title: The default secrets vendor is SOPS with age keys; committed encrypted files plus a project-held age key
context: ADR-901 fixes the contract; a project applying this blueprint still needs a working default vendor at day one. The rcf-lite tier this blueprint targets is small greenfield projects: a single deployable, one small team or one solo operator, no ops team standing by. A default vendor for that tier should ship with zero infrastructure to run, a small dependency footprint, an on-disk shape a human can read without a service running, and an integration surface a coding agent can use through a piped-stdin CLI without extra machinery. Larger deployments will supersede this decision; the point of a default is that day one works.
decision: The default vendor is Mozilla SOPS with age keys. Encrypted value files live under a project-authored path (typically `secrets/<environment>/<name>.enc`) committed to the repo; the age private key that decrypts them is a per-machine key held out of the repo (developer laptop keyring, CI runner secret, deployment host key material). The vendor adapter shape is: `readMany` shells to `sops --decrypt` on the resolved path per entry; `lastRotatedAt` is read from a `sops-metadata:` block the encrypt operation stamps; `materialiseCredentials` is a no-op because the SOPS invocation itself relies on the caller's age key. The default is chosen because it makes the zero-infrastructure floor real: no server to run, no account to hold, no per-project vault to provision. Projects that outgrow the default supersede this ADR with a project-level ADR selecting a hosted or self-hosted alternative (see alternatives).
consequences: The project ships with a working secrets flow on day one and does not force an ops decision before the first commit. The age key is now a first-class piece of operator state a project must manage (a key on every developer laptop, a key on every CI runner, a key on every host running the app); losing every copy of the key loses access to every committed encrypted file, which is a recoverable-by-rewrite problem for a project pre-launch and a recoverable-by-re-issue problem thereafter. The rotation-days gate reads a metadata block SOPS itself writes; a project that hand-edits the encrypted files bypasses the metadata and loses the gate's truth source. Composition with a vendor-specific superseding blueprint (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Doppler, Infisical) is a project-level ADR change and a vendor-adapter swap; the ADR-901 contract stays intact.

alternativesConsidered.name: HashiCorp Vault
alternativesConsidered.summary: Run a Vault server (self-hosted or Vault Cloud); the vendor adapter reads through the Vault HTTP API using an app-scoped token or an auth method.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: Reserved as the primary promotion path for projects that outgrow the SOPS default. Vault is the reference open-source posture for organisations with dedicated ops capacity: dynamic secrets, richer audit, policy engine, mature rotation orchestration. The trade against SOPS is running the server (or paying for the hosted plan) and the operator learning curve; small greenfield rcf-lite projects rarely need that day one.

alternativesConsidered.name: AWS Secrets Manager / GCP Secret Manager / Azure Key Vault
alternativesConsidered.summary: Hosted per-cloud secrets managers; the vendor adapter reads through the cloud SDK using workload-identity credentials.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: Ties the project to one cloud at the secrets layer; the doctrine of ADR-901 keeps the contract vendor-agnostic on purpose. Excellent choice for a project already committed to one cloud and using workload-identity; a project-level ADR supersede is the intended path there.

alternativesConsidered.name: Doppler / Infisical / other hosted third-party secrets services
alternativesConsidered.summary: Hosted vendor with a project workspace and per-environment scoping; the vendor adapter reads through the vendor's HTTP API using a service token.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: Same trade as the cloud-native option: a fine promotion path for a project that wants a managed service without cloud lock-in, but not the zero-infrastructure day-one default. A project-level ADR supersedes this ADR when the operator adopts one.

alternativesConsidered.name: Plaintext values in the repo
alternativesConsidered.summary: Commit secrets as plain files; ignore the encryption layer entirely.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: Fails every requirement in this blueprint that touches secret secrecy. Named only to explain why 'just put the secret in a file' is not the same shape as SOPS+age.
